title: Oxidative phosphorylation and chemiosmosis; Light-dependent reactions
specRef: C1.1(b); C1.1(a), C1.1(c), C1.1-SP1, C1.2(b) and others
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Eduqas A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: RS03b#t1 term and clue written for the game; RS03b#t3 term and clue written for the game; RS03b#t2 term and clue written for the game; PS02a#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: PS02a#N.4a, RS03b#N.4a, PS02a#N.7a, RS03b#N.9a, PS02a#N.8, PS02a#N.12a.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Photophosphorylation
items.clue: Name for ATP production in a chloroplast driven by light.

items.label: ATP synthase
items.clue: Enzyme in the thylakoid membrane through which H⁺ flow back out.

items.label: Stroma
items.clue: Chloroplast compartment that H⁺ are pumped out of and where the ATP is made.

items.label: Photolysis
items.clue: Splitting of water into H⁺, electrons and O₂, replacing the electrons lost from PSII.

questions.stem: Which statement about the photolysis of water in photosystem II is correct?

options.text: Light absorbed directly by water molecules in the thylakoid lumen breaks them apart into hydrogen gas and oxygen gas.
The hydrogen released from water is passed straight to NADP at photosystem II, reducing it before the electrons move on.
Its electrons replace those lost by the reaction centre, its protons join the gradient and oxygen is waste.
Oxygen is the useful product of photolysis, and the protons and electrons are waste that diffuses out of the chloroplast.

questions.explanation: Photolysis yields electrons, which replace those emitted by the reaction-centre chlorophyll, and protons, released into the thylakoid lumen. The oxygen is a waste product that diffuses away.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes how ATP is produced in the thylakoid?

options.text: Reduced NADP passes its electrons to the carriers, which pump protons for ATP synthesis, exactly as reduced NAD does in mitochondria.
The electron carriers make ATP directly as electrons pass along them, transferring the energy of each electron into a phosphate bond on ADP.
Protons are pumped out of the lumen into the stroma and flow back into the lumen through ATP synthase, releasing ATP inside it.
Electron carriers pump protons into the thylakoid lumen, and the protons flow back into the stroma through ATP synthase, which makes ATP.

questions.explanation: Energy from excited electrons passing along the carriers pumps protons into the lumen; ATP synthase uses their flow back into the stroma to phosphorylate ADP.

questions.stem: Which processes in an illuminated chloroplast build up the proton gradient across the thylakoid membrane?

options.text: Electron transport chain pumping, photolysis inside the thylakoid, and NADP reduction in the stroma
Only pumping by the electron transport chain, since photolysis releases its protons into the stroma
ATP synthase, which uses ATP to pump protons from the stroma into the thylakoid space
Reducing NADP, which releases protons into the thylakoid space

questions.explanation: All three raise [H⁺] inside the thylakoid relative to the stroma: two add H⁺ inside, one removes H⁺ outside.

questions.stem: A chemical is added that makes the thylakoid membrane freely permeable to protons, so that no proton gradient can build up across it. The chloroplasts are illuminated with a supply of ADP, phosphate and NADP. Which prediction is correct?

options.text: ATP is still made, because the electron carriers phosphorylate ADP directly as the electrons pass along.
Oxygen and reduced NADP continue to be produced in the light, but ATP synthesis stops completely.
Everything stops, because without ATP the photosystems have no energy to emit electrons.
More ATP is made, because the protons now reach ATP synthase in the stroma more quickly than before.

questions.stem: In illuminated chloroplasts of a hypothetical alga, the pH of the thylakoid space was 5.0 and the pH of the stroma was 8.0. What is the H⁺ concentration in the thylakoid space as a multiple of the H⁺ concentration in the stroma?

options.text: 3 times
1000 times
30 times
0.001 times

questions.explanation: Each pH unit is a tenfold difference. The thylakoid space is 3.0 units lower, so its H⁺ concentration is 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000 times greater: a steep gradient built by electron transport.

questions.stem: A chemical is added that takes electrons from photosystem I in place of NADP. The chloroplasts are illuminated with a supply of water, ADP, phosphate and NADP. Which prediction is correct?

options.text: ATP synthesis stops, because ATP is made only when electrons reach NADP.
Oxygen release stops, because water is split only when NADP is being reduced.
Oxygen is still released and ATP still made, but no reduced NADP forms.
Everything stops, because the photosystems need reduced NADP before they can emit electrons.

questions.explanation: Electrons still flow from water through PSII, the chain and PSI, so photolysis and proton pumping continue. Only the final acceptor has changed.
